newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Downward leg in NZ rates not over yet - BNZ report.
newsitem.headline: Downward leg in NZ rates not over yet - BNZ report.

text.p: The downward leg in New Zealand interest rates is not over, the Bank of New Zealand said in its November Quarterly outlook published on Tuesday.

In a "cautiously bullish" forecast, the bank said even the delayed formation of a government will not prevent 10 year bond yields falling as low as 6.75 percent from 7.15 percent and 90-day bank bills dropping to 8.0-8.25 percent from 8.9 percent.
It expects the spread against U.S. 10-year bonds will narrow to 50 basis points this quarter from 85 points at present.
While it believes inflation pressures will drop in the short-term, it believes the run down in inflation will be short-lived.

There will be some improvement in the annual underlying inflation rate for the next 2-4 quarters but BNZ expects the fall in inflation to be less than the Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) forecasts and to be less sustainable.
BNZ said the RBNZ's optimistic inflation outlook is based on house prices falling 5 percent to the end of 1997. But BNZ expects an improvement in house prices in late 1996 and 1997.

Despite a predicted monetary policy easing in December, New Zealand rates will continue to attract interest from Europe and Japan although interest will slow in the New Year as expectations of rate increases in Japan and Europe rise.
There is a risk the RBNZ's six monthly monetary policy statement on December 17 will merely sanction a fall in rates to date rather than be willing to accept further falls, BNZ said.
The New Zealand dollar would remain well supported "and there remains scope for further appreciation in the short-term with buyers everywhere and precious little supply".
It forecasts the New Zealand dollar to trade a US70-72 cent range and the Trade-Weighted Index to trade 66.5-68.5.
BNZ predicts the external sector will continue to struggle under the higher exchange rate and flat commodity prices ensuring the currency account deteriorates further.
BNZ said the economy grew an estimated 0.3 percent in the the third quarter and from the current quarter activity looked set to improve, albeit slowly at first.

Fiscal surpluses forecast forecast for 1999 and 2000 will not come about, BNZ predicts. Treasury growth forecasts are too optimistic and secondly, when a government is formed, it will increase spending.

New Zealand has a caretaker National Party conservative government after inconclusive elections last month, and the nationalist New Zealand First party, which holds the balance of power, is negotiating with both National and Labour over the shape of the next government.
BNZ said the real threats to the surpluses were the state of the economy and a sharper-than-expected slowdown of the economy in two to four years. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
